column2: Then the king, pacified and instructed by Brahmins, took his bow and went to another country with banner and chariot.
Having conquered the Narmada bank, Ekala, Mrittikavati and the mountain Riksha, he settled at Shuktimati.
Jyamagha's wife was the mighty, virtuous Shaibya; though childless, that king found no other wife.
He won a victory in battle and there obtained a maiden; frightened, the lord of men told his wife, "She is your daughter-in-law."
Hearing this the queen said, "Whose daughter-in-law, lord?" Hearing that, Jyamagha, best of kings, replied:
She is the wife arranged for the son who will be born to you.
By her fierce austerity, the fortunate Shaibya, grown old, bore a son, Vidarbha, on that maiden.
Of the princess, his daughter-in-law, Vidarbha afterwards begot two learned sons, Kratha and Kaishika, heroes skilled in battle.
Vidarbha's son was Bhima, whose son was Kunti; Kunti's son was Dhrishta, born mighty in battle.
Dhrishta had three heroic, exceedingly righteous sons: Avanta, Dasharha and the mighty Vishahara.
Dasharha's son was Vyoma; Vyoma's is called Jimuta; Jimuta's son Vikriti; his, remembered, Bhimaratha.
Bhimaratha's son was Navaratha; his son Dasharatha; his son Shakuni.
From him Karambha; Karambha's son was King Devarata; his Devakshatra; his Vriddhakshatra, of great fame.
Devakshatra's son was born like Devagarbha: the king Madhu, line-maker of the Madhus, sweet-spoken.
Then Purudvan, best of men, was born to Madhu on a Vidarbha woman; Madhu had an Aikshvaki wife, and on her was born
Satvan, endowed with all virtues, Satvata, increaser of fame. Knowing this creation of the great-souled Jyamagha, one who attends to it with great love will always be rich in offspring.
Kaushalya bore Satvata's sons, endowed with sattva: Bhagin, Bhajamana, the divine king Devavridha,
the mighty-armed Andhaka and Vrishni, the delight of Yadu. Their four branches have been told here in detail.
Bhajamana had two wives, Srinjayi — Bahya and Upabahyaka; from them many sons were born.
Krimi, Kramana, Dhrishta, Shura, Purañjaya: these were born of Bhajamana on Bahyaka-Srinjayi.
Ayutajit, Sahasrajit, Shatajit and Dasaka were born of Bhajamana on Upabahyaka-Srinjayi.
The sacrificer king Devavridha performed vast austerity, resolved: "May I have a son endowed with all virtues."
Joined with austerity, touching the water of the Parnasha river constantly, he was pleased by the river, who acted to please him.
Overcome by thought, she did not come to a decision; because of the king's goodness, that best of rivers
did not find any woman by whom he could have such a son. "Therefore I myself shall go and become his, with my followers."
Then, becoming a maiden bearing a supreme form, she chose the king, and the lord desired her.
He placed in her a radiant embryo, the noble-minded one. Then in the tenth month that best of rivers bore
a son, endowed with all virtues, Babhru Devavridha, Brahmins. About this line the knowers of the Puranas sing what is famed:

Reciting the virtues of the great-souled Devavridha, as we have seen from afar so we see from near:
brahmapuran:15:43	Babhru is the best of men, Devavridha equal to the gods; sixty-six men, and seven thousand,
brahmapuran:15:44	attained immortality through Babhru and Devavridha — the sacrificer, lord of gifts, wise, devoted to Brahmins, of firm weapons.
His line was very great: the Bhojas, those descended from Sartikavata. Andhaka on a Kashi princess had four sons:
Kukura, Bhajamana, Shashaka and Balabarhisha. Kukura's son was Vrishti, and Vrishti's son —
Kapotaroma; then Tilira was his son; from him Punarvasu was born, and from Punarvasu, Abhijit.
A pair of children was born to Abhijit: Ahuka and Shrahuka, the two best among the famed.
About that Ahuka they recite this verse: "With a white retinue, great, like a youth,
Ahuka, joined with eighty armours, should go first. Not one without a son, not without a hundred, not without a thousand-hundred years of life,
not of impure deeds, not a non-sacrificer — none such should approach the Bhoja. In the eastern direction, it is said, the Bhoja's elephants went,
from Soma, with ten thousand chariots with banners and armour, with sounds like clouds,
with twenty-one thousand golden-and-silver girdles; so many thousands too in the northern direction."
The Bhojas, kings of the earth, bear bowstrings and bells. The Andhakas, they say, gave a sister to the Avantis.
Ahuka had two sons on a Kashi princess: Devaka and Ugrasena, both like Devagarbha.
Devaka had four sons like the thirty gods: Devavan, Upadeva, Sandeva and Devarakshita.
He had seven daughters, whom he gave to Vasudeva: Devaki, Shantideva, Sudeva, Devarakshita,
Vrikadevi, Upadevi, and Sunamni the seventh. Ugrasena had nine sons, of whom Kamsa was the eldest:
Nyagrodha, Sunama, Kanka, Subhushana, Rashtrapala, Sutanu and the strong Anavrishti.
They had five sisters: Kamsa, Kamsavati, Sutanu, Rashtrapali and the excellent Kanka.
Ugrasena with his offspring, born of Kukura, has been described, upholding this line of the Kukuras of immeasurable might.
A man with offspring would obtain a vast line of his own.
He went to the water's edge to touch water and to worship the Sun; as he worshipped the Sun, Vivasvan stood before him,
the lord, in clear form, with a circle of brilliance. Then the king spoke to Vivasvan standing before him:

As I always see you in the sky, lord of lights, a god with a circle of splendour, so you stand before me.
brahmapuran:16:17	What difference is there between you and me, who have come by friendship? Hearing this, the revered one
took off from his neck the jewel Syamantaka and set it down aside. Then the king saw him in bodily form.
Pleased, Satrajit conversed with him for a moment; and as Vivasvan was about to depart again he said:
With which you constantly illumine all the worlds, lord — that jewel you ought to give me, revered one.
Then the Sun gave the Syamantaka jewel; tying it on, that king entered the city.
People ran after him, saying "The Sun is coming!" He entered his own city and the inner apartments amazed.
The king Satrajit lovingly gave that divine, excellent jewel Syamantaka to his brother Prasenajit.
The jewel yields gold in the Vrishni-Andhaka dwellings, rain comes in due season, and there was no fear of disease.
Govinda desired the Syamantaka jewel for Prasena; though able, he did not obtain it nor take it.
Once Prasena, adorned with it, went hunting and, for the sake of the Syamantaka, met his death from a forest-roving lion.
Then the mighty bear-king killed the charging lion, took that jewel and entered a cave.
Then the Vrishnis and Andhakas, because of Prasena's death and Krishna's earlier request for the jewel, all suspected Krishna.
Suspected, the righteous one resolved to clear himself of that deed and went to the forest, vowing, "I shall bring the jewel."
Where Prasena had hunted, he followed Prasena's tracks with trustworthy men.
Searching the best mountain Riksha-vat and the excellent Vindhya, the great-minded one, wearied, saw
Prasena slain with his horse, but did not find the jewel; and the lion not far from Prasena's body,
killed by a bear, shown by the bear's footprints. Following those tracks Madhava went to the bear's cave.
In the bear's den he heard words of a nurse, Brahmins, who with the child, Jambavan's son, was playing with the jewel and saying "Don't cry":
she was soothing him, saying "Don't cry."
The lion killed Prasena; the lion was killed by Jambavan. Little child, do not cry: this Syamantaka is yours.
At the clear sound he went quickly to the cave; the lord entering that bear's cave easily,
left the Yadavas with Langali (Balarama) at the cave's mouth. The bow-wielder saw Jambavan inside the cave.
Vasudeva fought with Jambavan in the cave with arms alone for twenty-one days.
When Krishna had entered the cave, those led by Baladeva went to Dvaravati and reported Krishna dead.
Vasudeva, having conquered the mighty Jambavan, obtained the bear-king's approved daughter Jambavati,
and took the Syamantaka jewel for his own clearing. Appeasing the bear-king, he came out of the cave.
Krishna came to Dvaraka with modest followers in front. Thus Achyuta, having brought the jewel and cleared himself,
gave it to Satrajit in the assembly of all the Satvatas. Thus Krishna, falsely accused, destroyer of foes,
was cleansed of the sin, having won back the Syamantaka. Satrajit had ten wives, and a hundred sons by them.
Three of them were famous: Bhagamkara the eldest, the hero Vatapati and Vasumedha;
and three daughters, famed in all directions, best of Brahmins: Satyabhama the best of them, Vratini and Dridhavrata,
and Prasvapini; he gave her as wife to Krishna. Sabhaksha, Bhangakara and Naveya were excellent men,
born endowed with virtue and famed for beauty. Then Madri's son was born, and Vrishni's son Yudhajit.
Vrishni had two sons, Shvaphalka and Chitraka. Shvaphalka found a Kashi king's daughter as wife,
named Gandini, to whom her father always gave cows; on her was born the mighty-armed Shrutavan, fond of guests,
and the fortunate Akrura, giver of ample fees; Upamadgu, Madgu, Mudara and Arimardana,
Arikshepa, Upeksha, Shatruha, Arimejaya, Dharmabhrit and Dharma, Gridhrabhoja and Andhaka,
Avaha, Prativaha, and the excellent woman Sundari; the queen of Vishrutashva and her daughter Vasundhara,
endowed with beauty and youth, charming to all beings. Akrura, on Ugrasena's daughter, had two sons, delights of the family:
Vasudeva and Upadeva, born radiant as gods. Chitraka's sons were Prithu and Viprithu,
Ashvagriva, Ashvabahu, Suparshvaka and Gaveshana, Arishtanemi; and his sons Dharma and Dharmabhrit,
Subahu, Bahubahu, and the two women Shravishtha and Shravana. He who knows this false accusation of Krishna as it has been told
is never touched by false accusations.
Then a tumultuous battle began between Bhoja (Shatadhanva) and Krishna. Shatadhanva then looked for Akrura on every side.
Seeing those two, Bhoja and Janardana, enraged there, Akrura, though able, because of a curse did not support Hardikya (Kritavarman).
Then Bhoja, afflicted with fear, decided to flee; he went more than a hundred yojanas on (the mare) Hridaya.
Hridaya, famed, was Bhoja's mare, Brahmins, who covers a hundred yojanas, by whom he fought Krishna.
Seeing Hridaya exhausted by speed at a hundred yojanas of the road, and his chariot's growth (reach), Krishna pressed Shatadhanva.
Then, from fatigue and distress, her life-breath rose to the sky when she was killed, Brahmins; then Krishna said to Rama:
Stay here, mighty-armed one; I have seen the mare's fault. I shall go on foot and take the jewel Syamantaka.
Going on foot, Achyuta, supreme knower of weapons, killed Shatadhanva near Mithila, Brahmins.
Having killed the mighty Bhoja he did not see the Syamantaka; Langali said to the returned Krishna, "Give the jewel."
There is none, said Krishna; then Rama, filled with anger, repeatedly answered Janardana with reproaches.
Because of brotherhood I forgive this. Farewell, I go. I have nothing to do with Dvaraka, with you, or with the Vrishnis.
Then Rama, the crusher of foes, entered Mithila and was honoured by the king of Mithila with all desired things.
At that very time Babhru, best of the wise, performed all kinds of sacrifices without restraint.
The wise, greatly famed son of Gandini entered a coat of mail made of initiation for protection, for the sake of the Syamantaka.
Then the righteous-souled one devoted other jewels and various wealth to sacrifices for sixty years.
They are famed as the Akrura sacrifices of that great-souled one, all with much food and fees, granting all desires.
Then King Duryodhana, the lord, went to Mithila and obtained from Baladeva divine instruction in the mace.
Then Rama, appeased, was brought to Dvaraka by the great Vrishni-Andhaka chariot-warriors and the great-souled Krishna.
And Akrura, bull among men, mighty, came with the Andhakas, having killed Satrajit asleep along with his kin.
For fear of division among kin, Krishna then ignored him. When Akrura had left, Indra did not rain.
Through lack of rain the kingdom became much weakened; then the Kukuras and Andhakas appeased Akrura.
When that lord of gifts had returned to Dvaravati, the thousand-eyed one then rained at the ocean's side.
Akrura, the wise, gave a maiden, his well-regarded sister, to Vasudeva for affection, best of sages.
Then Krishna, knowing by yoga that the jewel was with Babhru, said to Akrura in the middle of the assembly:

That excellent jewel which is in your hand, lord — give it, honoured one, and do not treat me dishonourably.
brahmapuran:17:37	The anger that arose in me after sixty years, sinless one, has grown and repeatedly come, and a great delay has passed.
Then at Krishna's word, in the assembly of all the Satvatas, the great-minded Babhru gave that jewel without difficulty.
Then Krishna, subduer of foes, glad-minded, gave that jewel, received in honesty from Babhru's hand, back to Babhru.
Gandini's son, wearing the jewel Syamantaka received from Krishna's hand, shone like the sun.
Himavan, Hemakuta and Nishadha lie to its south; Nila, Shveta and Shringi to the north are the boundary mountains of the varshas.
Two in the middle are a hundred thousand (yojanas) in measure, the others ten less each; they are two thousand high and equally broad.
Bharata is the first varsha, then Kimpurusha is remembered, and Harivarsha too, south of Meru, Brahmins.
Ramyaka is the northern varsha, and Hiranmaya of it too; the northern Kurus are like Bharata.
Each of these, best of Brahmins, is nine thousand (yojanas); in their middle is Ilavrita, where the golden Meru rises.
On all four sides of Meru there, fortunate ones, Ilavrita is nine thousand wide; and four mountains are here:
the wide supports of Meru, ten thousand yojanas broad. In the east is Mandara, in the south Gandhamadana,
in the west side Vipula, and in the north Supārshva stands. On them are the kadamba, jambu, pippala and banyan,
trees a thousand and a hundred yojanas high, standing as the mountains' banners. The jambu tree of Jambudvipa is the reason for its name, best of Brahmins.
The fruits of that jambu are the size of great elephants; they fall and burst everywhere on the mountain's back.
From their juice a river there called Jambunadi flows, and it is drunk by the dwellers there.
No distress, no foul smell, no old age, no decay of the senses occurs among people there whose minds are healthy by drinking it.
The bank-clay, receiving its juice and dried by the pleasant wind, becomes the gold called Jambunada, ornament of the Siddhas.
Bhadrashva lies east of Meru and Ketumala west; these are two varshas, best of sages, and between them Ilavrita.
In the east is the Chaitraratha forest, in the south Gandhamadana, in the west Vaibhraja, and likewise in the north Nandana is remembered.
Arunoda, Mahabhadra, Asitoda and Manasa: these four lakes are always enjoyed by the gods.
Shantavan, Chakrakunja, Kurari, Malyavan, Vaikanka and others are the Kesara mountains east of Meru.
Trikuta, Shishira, Patanga, Ruchaka, Nishadha and others are its southern Kesara mountains.
Shikhivasa, Vaidurya, Kapila, Gandhamadana, Janudhi and others are likewise the western Kesara mountains.
Next to Meru they stand at Jathara and others; Shankhakuta, Rishabha, Hamsa, Naga and others,
and Kalanjara and others are the northern Kesara mountains. A great city of fourteen thousand yojanas
on top of Meru in heaven, best of Brahmins, is told to be Brahma's. Around it in the eight directions and intermediate directions
are the famed excellent cities of the world-guardians beginning with Indra. Coming forth from Vishnu's foot, flooding the lunar disc,
the Ganga falls from heaven all around Brahma's city. Falling there she became fourfold in the directions:
Sita, Alakananda, Chakshu and Bhadra, in order. Sita in the east goes through the air from mountain to mountain,
and then flows with the eastern varsha, Bhadrashva, to the ocean; likewise Alakananda goes south and comes to Bharata,
